subject: Woodwork
practicalPaper: Paper 3 is a 3-hour practical test for 100 marks in which candidates make a test piece from supplied drawings. Marks are given for accurate preparation of stock to size, marking out, well-fitted joints, correct assembly (square and flat), surface finish and safe working; design and working-drawing skills are tested in Paper 2 Section B.

practicals.title: Preparing stock to size by hand
practicals.aim: To plane a piece of sawn timber to a given finished size with a true face side, face edge, width and thickness.
materials: Sawn hardwood or softwood (e.g. obeche or mahogany) slightly oversize
safety: Keep the plane blade retracted when not in use and lay the plane on its side.
Clamp the work securely; keep both hands behind the cutting edge.
procedure: Select the best face; plane it flat and out of winding; check with a straight edge and winding strips; mark the face-side symbol.
Plane the best edge straight and square to the face side; check with a try square; mark the face-edge symbol.
Gauge the width from the face edge on both faces and plane down to the lines.
Gauge the thickness from the face side all round and plane down to the lines.
Square one end with a knife line and saw/plane to it.
Measure the length from the squared end, square round and cut to length.
Check all dimensions and squareness.
practicals.expectedObservations: The piece is flat, square and to the drawn dimensions within about ±0.5 mm, with the face marks clearly shown.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Finished size 450 × 70 × 20 mm. Allow about 3–5 mm on width and thickness and 15–20 mm on length for planing and squaring: order sawn stock about 470 × 75 × 25 mm.
precautions: Plane with the grain to avoid tearing.
Always gauge from the face side or face edge.
Set the plane for a fine cut when nearing the line.
examTips: Examiners check size, flatness and squareness first; accurate stock preparation affects every joint mark.
Show the face-side and face-edge marks on your test piece.

checkQuestions.q: The first surface to be prepared is the
checkQuestions.explanation: All other surfaces are referenced from it.

checkQuestions.q: Winding strips are used to check for
checkQuestions.explanation: They show whether a surface is twisted.

checkQuestions.q: Width and thickness are marked with a
checkQuestions.explanation: The gauge scribes a line parallel to the face.

practicals.title: Ripping and cross-cutting
practicals.aim: To cut timber along the grain (ripping) and across the grain (cross-cutting) accurately with hand saws.
safety: Support the work so it does not pinch the saw or fall.
Keep the free hand away from the saw path; start the cut with the thumb guiding the blade.
procedure: Mark the cutting lines with a knife (cross-cut) or gauge/pencil (rip).
Place the board on trestles; start the cut on the waste side of the line with short strokes.
Rip with the saw at about 60° to the board; cross-cut at about 45°.
Keep the saw vertical; check with a try square.
Support the off-cut near the end to avoid splitting.
Plane or pare to the line and check the cut.
practicals.expectedObservations: Cuts are straight, square and just on the waste side of the line, needing minimal cleaning up.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Rip saw teeth are chisel-shaped (about 4–5 points per 25 mm); cross-cut teeth are knife-pointed (about 6–8 points per 25 mm). A saw kerf of about 2 mm must be allowed when cutting several pieces from one board: four pieces of 300 mm need 4 × 300 + 4 × 2 = 1 208 mm.
precautions: Cut on the waste side of the line.
Use the full length of the saw blade.
commonMistakes: Cutting on the line, leaving the piece undersize.
examTips: Name saws and their uses; sketch rip and cross-cut teeth.
Neat, square cuts improve joint fit marks.

checkQuestions.q: Ripping means cutting
checkQuestions.explanation: Rip saws cut along the grain.

checkQuestions.q: Cross-cut saw teeth are shaped like
checkQuestions.explanation: They sever the fibres across the grain.

checkQuestions.q: Why cut on the waste side of the line?
options: So the piece stays full size
checkQuestions.explanation: The kerf is removed from waste, not work.

practicals.title: Constructing a through mortise and tenon joint
practicals.aim: To mark out, cut and fit a through mortise and tenon joint used in framing.
safety: Clamp work over a solid part of the bench when chopping mortises.
Keep hands behind the chisel edge.
procedure: Mark the shoulder line of the tenon all round with a knife.
Set the mortise gauge to the chisel width (about one-third of the stock thickness) and gauge both tenon and mortise from the face side.
Chop the mortise from both edges towards the centre, keeping the chisel vertical.
Saw the tenon cheeks on the waste side, then the shoulders.
Pare the tenon to fit; test-fit without forcing.
Check the frame for square, then glue and cramp.
practicals.expectedObservations: The tenon slides in with hand pressure, shoulders close tightly and the frame is square.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Tenon thickness ≈ ⅓ of stock thickness: for 25 mm stock, 25/3 = 8.3 mm → use an 8 mm mortise chisel. Tenon width for a 50 mm rail is often reduced (haunched) at frame ends.
precautions: Gauge from the face side for both parts.
Chop halfway from each side to avoid splitting out.
sourcesOfError: Chisel not vertical, giving a sloping mortise.
examTips: Joint fit and shoulder closure carry high marks in the test piece.
Sketch the joint in isometric with parts labelled.

checkQuestions.q: Tenon thickness is usually about
checkQuestions.explanation: This keeps both parts strong.

checkQuestions.q: The mortise is chopped with a
checkQuestions.explanation: A strong chisel withstands levering.

checkQuestions.q: The mortise and tenon is mainly a
checkQuestions.explanation: It is used in doors, tables and frames.

practicals.title: Constructing a common through dovetail joint
practicals.aim: To mark out and cut a common through dovetail joint for box construction.
safety: Secure work in the vice; keep hands behind chisels.
procedure: Gauge the thickness of each board on the other around the ends.
Mark the tails with a 1:6 (softwood) or 1:8 (hardwood) slope using the template.
Saw down the tails on the waste side; remove waste with coping saw and chisel.
Use the tails to mark the pins on the second board with a knife.
Saw and chop out the pins.
Test-fit, pare carefully, glue and check square.
practicals.expectedObservations: The tails and pins fit snugly without gaps and the box corner is square.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Slope 1:6 corresponds to an angle of tan⁻¹(1/6) ≈ 9.5°; slope 1:8 ≈ 7.1°. A gentler slope is used for hardwood because it is stronger and resists crushing.
precautions: Mark tails first and transfer to pins.
Saw on the waste side.
sourcesOfError: Inaccurate transfer of tails to pins.
examTips: Name dovetail types: common, lapped, secret; give their uses.
Show slope ratios in sketches.

checkQuestions.q: The dovetail slope for hardwood is about
checkQuestions.explanation: Hardwood uses 1:8, softwood 1:6.

checkQuestions.q: Dovetail joints are mainly used in
checkQuestions.explanation: They resist pulling apart in one direction.

checkQuestions.q: Which is normally cut first?
checkQuestions.explanation: Tails are cut first and used to mark the pins.

practicals.title: Constructing housing and halving joints
practicals.aim: To cut a through housing joint for shelf-like construction and a cross-halving joint for frames.
safety: Clamp work firmly before sawing and chiselling.
procedure: Mark the housing width using the shelf itself; square lines across with a knife.
Gauge the housing depth (about one-third of the board thickness).
Saw down the sides of the housing to depth.
Remove waste with chisel and router plane to a flat bottom.
For halving, mark half the thickness from the face of each piece and cut each to a depth of half.
Test-fit both joints and adjust.
practicals.expectedObservations: The shelf fits the housing without play; halving joint faces are flush.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: For 18 mm stock, housing depth ≈ 18/3 = 6 mm. For a 40 mm thick cross-halving, each part is cut to 40/2 = 20 mm deep so the faces finish flush.
precautions: Mark width from the actual piece, not a rule.
Check depth at both ends.
commonMistakes: Cutting the halving from the wrong face so the pieces do not finish flush.
examTips: Name each joint and its typical use: bookshelves (housing), frames (halving).
Sketch exploded views.

checkQuestions.q: A housing joint is used for
checkQuestions.explanation: Shelves sit in housings cut in uprights.

checkQuestions.q: For a halving joint in 30 mm stock, each part is cut
checkQuestions.explanation: Half the thickness.

checkQuestions.q: The tool for levelling the bottom of a housing is the
checkQuestions.explanation: It gives a uniform depth.

practicals.title: Edge jointing: dowelled and tongued-and-grooved widening joints
practicals.aim: To join narrow boards edge to edge to make a wide panel using dowels and a tongue-and-groove joint.
apparatus: Brace and dowel bit or drill
safety: Use the drill with the work clamped; wear goggles.
procedure: Arrange boards with alternating growth rings to reduce cupping; mark them.
Plane edges straight and square (shoot the edges) and check with a straight edge.
Mark dowel positions across both boards; drill with the jig.
For the T&G joint, plough a groove in one edge and form a matching tongue on the other.
Dry-assemble, then glue and cramp, alternating cramps above and below.
Wipe off squeezed glue and leave to set.
practicals.expectedObservations: A flat panel with tight, nearly invisible joint lines.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: For 20 mm boards, choose dowel diameter about ⅓–½ thickness: 8 mm. Dowel length ≈ 5 × diameter = 40 mm (20 mm into each board). Space dowels about 150 mm apart: a 600 mm joint needs about 4 dowels.
precautions: Alternate the heart side of boards.
Do not over-tighten cramps (starves the joint of glue).
commonMistakes: All cramps on one side, bowing the panel.
examTips: Name widening joints: butt (rubbed), dowelled, tongued and grooved, loose tongue, rebated.
Explain why growth rings are alternated.

checkQuestions.q: Boards for a panel are arranged with alternating heart sides to
checkQuestions.explanation: Opposing tendencies to cup balance out.

checkQuestions.q: A widening joint is used to
options: make wide boards from narrow ones
checkQuestions.explanation: It joins boards edge to edge.

checkQuestions.q: A 10 mm dowel is typically about
checkQuestions.explanation: About five times the diameter.

practicals.title: Assembling and gluing a frame and testing for squareness
practicals.aim: To carry out a trial assembly, glue up and cramp a frame, and test for squareness, flatness and parallelism.
materials: Cut joints for a rectangular frame (e.g. 600 × 400 mm)
safety: Tighten cramps evenly; keep fingers clear of cramp jaws.
procedure: Clean up inside edges before assembly.
Dry-assemble and cramp the frame.
Measure both diagonals; adjust cramps until they are equal.
Check flatness by sighting across or with winding strips.
Dismantle, apply glue to all joint surfaces and re-assemble.
Re-check diagonals and flatness; wipe off excess glue.
Leave to set, then flush off joints and clean up.
practicals.expectedObservations: Equal diagonals show the frame is square; it lies flat with no twist.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: For a 600 × 400 mm frame, each diagonal = √(600² + 400²) = √520 000 = 721.1 mm. If one diagonal is 724 mm and the other 718 mm, push the long-diagonal corners together (or skew the cramps) until both read 721 mm.
precautions: Protect work with cramp blocks.
Apply glue evenly but not excessively.
sourcesOfError: Cramp pressure pulling the frame out of square.
commonMistakes: Leaving dried glue on surfaces to be finished.
examTips: Mention trial assembly and the diagonal test in your answer.
Clean, square assembly earns high marks in the test piece.

checkQuestions.q: A frame is square when
checkQuestions.explanation: Equal diagonals prove right angles in a rectangle.

checkQuestions.q: Cramp blocks are used to
checkQuestions.explanation: They spread pressure and prevent bruising.

practicals.title: Determining the moisture content of timber
practicals.aim: To determine the moisture content of timber by the oven-dry method and compare it with a moisture meter reading.
materials: Timber samples (e.g. 25 mm slices cut at least 300 mm from board ends)
safety: Use oven gloves.
Keep the meter pins pointed away from hands.
procedure: Cut sample slices from the middle of the board, free of knots and away from the ends.
Remove splinters and weigh each sample immediately (wet mass).
Dry in the oven at 103 °C, weighing at intervals until the mass is constant (oven-dry mass).
Calculate the moisture content.
Take moisture meter readings on the parent board and compare.
State whether the timber is suitable for indoor furniture.
practicals.expectedObservations: Mass decreases on drying until it becomes constant. Fresh (green) timber may show over 30% MC; air-dried timber in Nigeria often settles around 15–20%.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: MC% = (wet mass − oven-dry mass)/oven-dry mass × 100. Wet = 250 g, dry = 200 g: MC = (250 − 200)/200 × 100 = 25%. A second sample: (48 − 40)/40 × 100 = 20%.
precautions: Weigh samples straight after cutting to avoid moisture loss.
Dry to constant mass.
sourcesOfError: Meter readings affected by species and temperature.
commonMistakes: Dividing by the wet mass instead of the dry mass.
examTips: State the formula with "oven-dry mass" in the denominator.
Give advantages: oven method accurate but slow and destructive; meter quick but less accurate.

checkQuestions.q: Wet mass 120 g, oven-dry 100 g. MC =
The oven temperature for the oven-dry method is about
checkQuestions.explanation: Water evaporates without charring the wood.

checkQuestions.q: Kiln seasoning compared with air seasoning is
checkQuestions.explanation: Kilns control temperature and humidity.

practicals.title: Identifying West African timbers
practicals.topic: West African Timbers in Common Use
practicals.aim: To identify common West African timbers from samples by colour, grain, texture, weight and smell, and state their uses.
materials: Labelled and unlabelled samples: iroko, mahogany, obeche (wawa), abura, afara, African walnut, mansonia, ebony, cedar
safety: Some dusts (e.g. mansonia, iroko) irritate the nose: avoid sanding samples without a mask.
procedure: Examine each sample for colour (heartwood/sapwood), grain (straight/interlocked), texture (fine/coarse) and figure.
Cut a clean end with the knife and view pores with the lens.
Weigh a measured block and calculate density.
Note smell and hardness (thumbnail test).
Identify the timber using a key and state two uses.
Record in a table.
practicals.expectedObservations: Obeche is pale and light; iroko is golden-brown darkening with age, heavy and durable; mahogany is reddish-brown with interlocked grain; ebony is black and very dense.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Block 300 × 50 × 50 mm = 0.3 × 0.05 × 0.05 = 0.00075 m³ with mass 0.55 kg: density = 0.55/0.00075 = 733 kg/m³ (medium-heavy, e.g. iroko range). Obeche is typically about 350–400 kg/m³.
precautions: Use dry samples; moisture affects colour and weight.
Examine a freshly cut surface.
examTips: Give local names alongside trade names (e.g. obeche = wawa, afromosia = kokrodua).
Pair each timber with a specific use (iroko – outdoor furniture, obeche – drawer sides/mouldings).

checkQuestions.q: Obeche (wawa) is
checkQuestions.explanation: It is a light, soft hardwood.

checkQuestions.q: A durable timber for outdoor use is
checkQuestions.explanation: Iroko resists decay and insects.

checkQuestions.q: Density is calculated as
checkQuestions.explanation: kg/m³.

practicals.title: Identifying timber defects
practicals.aim: To identify natural, seasoning, conversion and biological defects on timber samples and suggest causes and remedies.
materials: Timber samples showing knots, shakes, checks, cup, bow, twist, spring, wane, insect holes, fungal stain/rot
safety: Handle rotten or insect-infested samples with gloves and keep them away from sound timber.
procedure: Lay out samples and inspect each one.
Use the straight edge to detect bow, cup, spring and twist.
Identify knots (live/dead), shakes, checks and splits.
Identify wane and wrong sawing from conversion.
Identify insect and fungal attack.
Sketch each defect and record cause, prevention and remedy.
practicals.expectedObservations: Seasoning defects (cup, bow, twist, checks) come from uneven drying; dead knots may fall out; frass and holes show insect attack.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Measuring bow: a 2.0 m board touching a straight edge at its ends with a 12 mm gap at mid-length has a bow of 12 mm in 2 m, i.e. 6 mm per metre.
precautions: Inspect all four faces and both ends.
commonMistakes: Naming cup as bow (cup is across the width; bow along the length of the face).
examTips: Sketches of cup, bow, spring and twist are often asked; label clearly.
Group defects by cause.

checkQuestions.q: Curvature across the width of a board is
checkQuestions.explanation: Cup is across the face width.

checkQuestions.q: Wane is caused during
checkQuestions.explanation: It is bark or missing wood at the edge from sawing near the log surface.

checkQuestions.q: Small round holes with powdery dust indicate
checkQuestions.explanation: Beetle larvae leave frass.

practicals.title: Applying timber preservatives
practicals.aim: To apply a timber preservative by brushing and by dipping and to estimate the quantity required.
materials: Preservative (e.g. water-borne copper-based, or organic solvent type)
safety: Preservatives are toxic: wear gloves, goggles and respirator; work outdoors or with good ventilation.
No smoking near solvent preservatives.
Dispose of residues safely, away from water sources.
procedure: Ensure timber is dry and cut to final size before treatment.
Calculate surface area and preservative needed.
Brush two coats, paying attention to end grain.
Dip other samples for the stated time.
Stack treated timber to dry under cover.
Compare penetration on cut ends.
practicals.expectedObservations: Dipped samples show deeper and more even penetration than brushed ones; end grain absorbs most.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Ten battens 2.4 m × 150 × 50 mm: area of one = 2(2.4 × 0.15 + 2.4 × 0.05 + 0.15 × 0.05) = 0.975 m²; ten = 9.75 m². At a coverage of 8 m² per litre per coat: 9.75/8 = 1.22 L per coat, about 2.44 L for two coats.
precautions: Treat after final cutting, or re-treat cut ends.
Allow full drying before use.
examTips: Name methods: brushing, spraying, dipping, steeping, pressure (vacuum-pressure) impregnation, with pros and cons.
State properties of a good preservative: toxic to fungi/insects, permanent, penetrating, safe to handle, non-corrosive.

checkQuestions.q: The most effective preservation method listed is
checkQuestions.explanation: Pressure forces preservative deep into the timber.

checkQuestions.q: End grain should receive
checkQuestions.explanation: It absorbs moisture and decay organisms readily.

checkQuestions.q: An area of 16 m² at 8 m²/L per coat needs for one coat

practicals.title: Surface preparation and application of wood finishes
practicals.aim: To prepare a wood surface with abrasives and apply stain, filler and varnish (or French polish) to obtain a smooth finish.
safety: Ventilate the room; finishes and solvents are flammable and give off fumes.
Wear a dust mask when sanding.
Spread used polishing rags flat to dry (they can self-ignite if bundled).
procedure: Remove marks with a smoothing plane and cabinet scraper.
Sand with the grain using coarse, then medium, then fine grades on a block.
Remove dust with a tack cloth.
Apply stain evenly; wipe off excess; allow to dry.
Apply grain filler on open-grained timber and rub off across the grain.
Apply the first coat of varnish thinly; when dry, de-nib with fine paper.
Apply further coats and allow to harden.
practicals.expectedObservations: An even colour and smooth, glossy or satin film with no runs, dust or brush marks.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Abrasive grade numbers indicate grit per inch: higher numbers are finer. A typical sequence is 80 → 120 → 180 → 240; skipping from 80 straight to 240 leaves deep scratches that show under the finish.
precautions: Always sand with the grain.
Apply thin coats and allow full drying.
Work in a dust-free area.
examTips: Name finishes and their uses: polyurethane (hard-wearing), French polish (high-quality furniture), oil (outdoor/teak), paint.
Describe the stages in sequence.

checkQuestions.q: Which abrasive grade is finest?
checkQuestions.explanation: Higher grit numbers are finer.

checkQuestions.q: French polish is made from
checkQuestions.explanation: Shellac in spirit, applied with a rubber.

checkQuestions.q: Grain filler is used on
checkQuestions.explanation: It fills pores for a level finish.

practicals.title: Fitting butt hinges and a cabinet lock
practicals.aim: To recess and fit butt hinges and a cupboard lock to a small cabinet door.
materials: Pair of 50 mm brass butt hinges
safety: Pare towards the waste with hands behind the chisel.
procedure: Mark hinge positions (about one-sixth of the door height from top and bottom).
Gauge the leaf width and knuckle depth; mark the recess.
Saw and chop the recess; pare to depth.
Bore pilot holes; fix the hinges to the door, then to the carcass with one screw each; test and then fix fully.
Mark the lock position; cut the recess and keyhole; fit the lock.
Mark and fit the striking plate or recess in the carcass.
Check that the door swings freely and locks.
practicals.expectedObservations: The door closes flush with even gaps, hinges sit level with the surface and the lock operates smoothly.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Door height 600 mm: hinges about 600/6 = 100 mm from top and bottom. For a 15 mm thick door, screw length about 2.5 × 15 ≈ 38 mm into the carcass side; choose screws that do not break through the face of the door (e.g. 16 mm into the door edge).
precautions: Use matching screw gauges and countersink properly.
Fix with one screw first to allow adjustment.
sourcesOfError: Recesses too deep, causing binding (hinge-bound door).
commonMistakes: Screws too long, breaking through the face.
examTips: Name fittings and fasteners and sketch them: butt, tee and piano hinges; nails, screws, bolts, corrugated fasteners.
Explain pilot and clearance holes.

checkQuestions.q: A pilot hole is drilled for
options: the threaded part of the screw
checkQuestions.explanation: It prevents splitting and guides the screw.

checkQuestions.q: A door that springs open because hinges are recessed too deeply is
checkQuestions.explanation: Recesses too deep make the leaves bind.

checkQuestions.q: A long continuous hinge is a
checkQuestions.explanation: Piano hinges run the full length.

practicals.title: Sharpening and maintaining edge tools
practicals.aim: To grind and hone a plane iron and chisel to the correct angles and to carry out routine maintenance of hand tools.
apparatus: Bench grinder with tool rest and eye shield
safety: Wear goggles on the grinder; set the tool rest close to the wheel.
Do not overheat the edge (blue colour means lost temper); dip in water often.
procedure: Inspect the edge for nicks and squareness.
Grind the bevel at about 25° keeping the edge square to the sides.
Hone a secondary bevel at about 30° on the oilstone.
Remove the burr by rubbing the flat back on the stone.
Test sharpness on end grain.
Clean, oil and store tools; check plane mouth and cap iron.
practicals.expectedObservations: A sharp edge shaves end grain cleanly; the honed micro-bevel is visible as a narrow bright line.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Grinding angle 25° and honing angle 30°: the honing bevel is 5° steeper, so only a narrow strip at the tip needs honing each time, saving time.
precautions: Keep the stone lubricated and flat.
Use the whole stone surface.
sourcesOfError: Rocking the blade, rounding the bevel.
commonMistakes: Honing the back at an angle.
examTips: State types of maintenance: corrective, routine, predictive, preventive, with examples.
Give both angles: grinding 25°, honing 30°.

checkQuestions.q: The honing angle of a chisel is about
checkQuestions.explanation: Grinding about 25°, honing about 30°.

checkQuestions.q: A blue tint on a ground edge shows
options: the steel has lost its hardness
checkQuestions.explanation: Overheating draws the temper.

checkQuestions.q: Oiling tools after use is an example of
checkQuestions.explanation: It prevents rust before it occurs.

practicals.title: Safe use of the circular saw and surface planer
practicals.aim: To demonstrate safe set-up and operation of the circular saw bench and surface planer using guards, fences and push sticks.
apparatus: Circular saw bench with riving knife and crown guard
materials: Prepared softwood boards free of nails and loose knots
safety: Machines are used only under direct teacher supervision.
No loose clothing, ties or jewellery; tie back long hair.
Use push sticks for the last 300 mm of a cut; never reach over the blade.
Switch off and wait for the blade to stop before adjusting.
procedure: Inspect the machine, guards and blade; check the riving knife is aligned.
Set the blade height about 10 mm above the work and the fence to the width.
Stand to one side of the blade line; feed steadily with the face edge against the fence.
Finish the cut with a push stick.
On the surface planer, set the bridge guard just above the work and use push blocks.
Switch off, isolate and clean the machines.
practicals.expectedObservations: Clean, safe cuts with no kick-back; all guards remain in place throughout.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Peripheral speed of a 250 mm blade at 3 000 rev/min: v = π × 0.25 × 3 000 = 2 356 m/min ≈ 39 m/s — showing why hands must be kept well clear.
precautions: Check timber for nails and stones.
Never cross-cut freehand against the rip fence.
sourcesOfError: Blunt blades causing burning and kick-back.
commonMistakes: Standing in line with the blade.
examTips: List machine safety rules and the purpose of the riving knife.
Name machines with their uses: circular saw, band saw, thicknesser, mortiser, lathe.

checkQuestions.q: The riving knife on a circular saw prevents
checkQuestions.explanation: It keeps the kerf open behind the blade.

checkQuestions.q: A push stick is used
options: to feed the last part of the cut safely
checkQuestions.explanation: It keeps hands away from the blade.

checkQuestions.q: Before adjusting a machine you must
options: switch off and wait for it to stop
checkQuestions.explanation: Rotating parts are dangerous.

practicals.title: Turning between centres on the wood lathe
practicals.aim: To turn a cylindrical spindle (e.g. a tool handle or candle holder stem) between centres using gouges, skew chisel and parting tool.
apparatus: Wood lathe with driving centre and tailstock centre
Roughing gouge, spindle gouge, skew chisel, parting tool
materials: Square turning blank (e.g. abura or mahogany 50 × 50 × 250 mm)
safety: Wear a face shield; remove loose clothing.
Rotate the work by hand before switching on.
Keep the tool rest close to the work and adjust only when stopped.
procedure: Mark diagonals on the ends; centre punch.
Mount between centres; set tool rest about 5 mm from the corners.
Start at low speed and rough down to a cylinder with the roughing gouge.
Mark key diameters and set calipers; cut sizing grooves with the parting tool.
Shape beads and coves with the spindle gouge and skew.
Sand at low speed and apply finish.
Part off or remove and saw off waste ends.
practicals.expectedObservations: A smooth, symmetrical spindle with diameters matching the drawing.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Surface speed at 50 mm diameter and 2 000 rev/min: v = π × 0.05 × 2 000 = 314 m/min ≈ 5.2 m/s. A 300 mm bowl blank at the same surface speed should run at only about 318 rev/min, so larger work needs lower speeds.
precautions: Start slow for square or unbalanced blanks.
Keep tools sharp and the bevel rubbing.
commonMistakes: Adjusting the tool rest while running.
Presenting the skew flat, causing a catch.
examTips: Name lathe parts: headstock, tailstock, bed, tool rest, centres, face plate.
Distinguish faceplate turning and turning between centres.

checkQuestions.q: Large-diameter work on the lathe should be turned at
checkQuestions.explanation: Surface speed rises with diameter.

checkQuestions.q: Diameters are checked with
checkQuestions.explanation: Calipers transfer and check diameters.

checkQuestions.q: A bowl is usually turned using
checkQuestions.explanation: Faceplate turning suits bowls.

practicals.title: Working drawing and cutting list for a stool
practicals.aim: To produce a first-angle orthographic working drawing of a small stool with sections, and to prepare a cutting list and bill of materials with cost.
safety: Keep instruments protected and work area tidy.
procedure: Make freehand sketches of design ideas and select one.
Draw front elevation, end elevation and plan in first-angle projection at 1:5 (or as specified).
Add a section showing the joints and material hatching.
Dimension fully and add title block with projection symbol.
List every part in a cutting list: part, number, length, width, thickness, material.
Calculate the volume of timber and cost with a waste allowance.
practicals.expectedObservations: Views align correctly; dimensions are complete; the cutting list matches the drawing.
precautions: Use finished sizes in the cutting list and allow waste separately.
Draw the correct projection symbol.

practicals.title: Design and construction of a small project
practicals.aim: To identify a need, design a solution (e.g. a bedside cabinet or shoe rack), cost it, build it and evaluate it against the specification.
apparatus: Hand tools, portable power tools and machines as needed
safety: Follow all workshop and machine safety rules; wear PPE.
procedure: Write a design brief from a customer need or market survey.
Write a specification: size, function, material, finish, cost limit.
Sketch alternative ideas and choose the best with reasons.
Produce working drawings and a cutting list.
Estimate cost of materials, labour and overheads.
Construct the project, recording each stage.
Evaluate: test against the specification and suggest improvements.
practicals.expectedObservations: A finished product that meets the specification, with a design folio recording the process.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Costing example: materials ₦12 000, consumables ₦1 500, labour 8 h × ₦800 = ₦6 400, overheads 10% of (materials + labour) = ₦1 840. Total cost = 12 000 + 1 500 + 6 400 + 1 840 = ₦21 740. With 25% profit, selling price = ₦27 175.
precautions: Check measurements against the drawing at each stage.
Do trial assemblies.
examTips: Follow the design process in order: problem, brief, research, specification, ideas, solution, planning, making, evaluation.

practicals.title: Hammer veneering a panel
practicals.aim: To lay a decorative veneer on a groundwork panel by the hammer method.
safety: Handle hot glue carefully to avoid burns.
Cut veneer against a straight edge with fingers away from the blade.
procedure: Prepare the groundwork flat and key it with a toothing plane.
Cut the veneer slightly oversize.
Glue the groundwork; lay the veneer.
Warm with the iron to re-liquefy the glue and press out from the centre with the veneer hammer in zig-zag strokes.
Tape joints; check for blisters by tapping and re-press.
Veneer the back with a balancing veneer.
Trim edges when dry and clean up.
practicals.expectedObservations: Veneer lies flat with no blisters; tapping sounds solid all over.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Veneer area: a 600 × 400 mm panel needs 0.24 m² per face, and veneering both faces (face and balancing) needs 0.48 m², plus about 10% for trimming → 0.53 m².
precautions: Work from the centre outwards to expel glue and air.
Always balance-veneer the back to prevent warping.
examTips: Describe both hammer and caul/press methods.
Name veneering tools and uses.

checkQuestions.explanation: Equal pull on both faces prevents warping.

practicals.title: Relief carving of a simple motif
practicals.aim: To transfer a design to a board and carve it in low relief using carving tools.
materials: Fine-grained hardwood board (e.g. mahogany or abura)
safety: Clamp the work and keep both hands behind the cutting edge.
Carve away from the body.
procedure: Draw or trace the motif (e.g. a leaf or local symbol) onto the board.
Outline the motif with the V-tool (incising).
Set in the outline vertically with chisels and gouges.
Remove the background (grounding) to an even depth.
Model the raised motif with gouges to give form.
Clean up and apply a finish.
practicals.expectedObservations: The motif stands out evenly from a level background with clean outlines.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Ground depth is usually small in low relief: for a 25 mm board, a depth of about 5–6 mm (roughly one-fifth of the thickness) gives good shadow without weakening the board.
precautions: Cut with the grain where possible to avoid tearing.
Keep tools very sharp.
examTips: Distinguish incised and relief carving.
Sketch carving tools with uses.

practicals.title: Upholstering a padded stool seat
practicals.aim: To upholster a drop-in or fixed stool seat with webbing, padding and a fabric cover.
safety: Hold tacks in a magnetic hammer, not in the mouth.
Keep fingers clear of the staple gun.
procedure: Fix webbing across the frame in both directions, tensioned with the stretcher and interlaced.
Cover with hessian and tack down.
Cut foam slightly oversize and bevel the edges; fix in place.
Lay wadding over the foam.
Cut the cover with enough allowance; temporary tack at centres of each side.
Work outwards to the corners, pulling evenly; fold corners neatly.
Fix the bottom cloth and trim.
practicals.expectedObservations: A firm, smooth seat with even tension, neat corners and no wrinkles.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: For a 400 × 400 mm seat with 40 mm foam, cover size = seat size + 2 × (foam thickness + frame depth 25 mm + 30 mm turn-under) = 400 + 2 × 95 = 590 mm square.
precautions: Keep fabric grain straight.
Tension webbing evenly.
examTips: Name upholstery materials for framing, padding, covering and decoration.
Describe processes in order.

checkQuestions.explanation: Tight webbing supports the seat.

checkQuestions.explanation: This keeps the fabric square.

practicals.title: Laminated bending of a curved component
practicals.aim: To make a curved component by gluing thin laminates around a former.
materials: Thin laminates (2–3 mm) or constructional veneers
Plastic sheet to stop glue sticking to the former
safety: Wear gloves when using synthetic resin glue; ventilate.
Tighten cramps evenly.
procedure: Make the former to the curve required.
Cut laminates slightly over width and length.
Dry-cramp to check fit.
Spread glue on all mating faces.
Cramp the stack between formers from the centre outwards.
Leave to cure fully; remove and trim edges.
Clean up and finish.
practicals.expectedObservations: The curve holds its shape after removal with little spring-back; glue lines are thin and continuous.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: A 12 mm thick curved rail from 3 mm laminates needs 12/3 = 4 laminates. Thinner laminates allow a tighter radius but need more glue lines.
precautions: Use a former slightly tighter than required to allow for spring-back.
Ensure full glue coverage.
examTips: Compare solid (steam) bending with laminated bending.
Name suitable timbers for bending (e.g. ash-type, beech, or local flexible species) and give reasons.

checkQuestions.q: In laminated bending, curves are held by
checkQuestions.explanation: Glue lines lock the curve.

checkQuestions.explanation: More glue lines resist straightening.
